cards.explanation: The answer is thin. The text says these seven cows were “…sickly and thin…” (Genesis 41:3). They climb out of the Nile and stand right next to the sleek ones on the bank. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, later calls them “…sickly, ugly, and thin…” (Genesis 41:19). Seven healthy cows and seven skinny ones, side by side, and nobody's asking for a group photo.

The answer is False. The thin cows aren't the ones running anywhere. Genesis 41:4 says they “…devoured the seven sleek, well-fed cows.” Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wakes up right after that, and I'd say that makes sense.

The answer is that they swallow up the plump ones. Same move as the cows. Genesis 41:7 says “…the thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven plump, ripe ones.” Then Pharaoh, king of Egypt, wakes and realizes it was a dream. Two dreams, one pattern. The skinny ones keep winning.

The answer is troubled. The text says it plainly: “In the morning his spirit was troubled…” (Genesis 41:8). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, dreamed of thin cows devouring well-fed cows, then fell back asleep and dreamed of thin heads of grain swallowing plump ones (Genesis 41:4-7). I'd be rattled too, and he doesn't shrug it off. He summons the magicians and wise men of Egypt.

The answer is all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Genesis 41:8 says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “…summoned all the magicians and wise men of Egypt.” When his spirit is troubled, he doesn't text one guy. He calls the whole group chat. And still, the verse says no one could interpret the dreams for him.

The answer is False. Genesis 41:8 says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “…told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for him.” All those wise people in one room and nobody has an answer. I know that quiet room, friends, I've sat in a few.

The answer is the chief cupbearer. He speaks up to Pharaoh with “Today I recall my failures.” (Genesis 41:9). Then he tells the king about a young Hebrew who interpreted his dream and the chief baker's dream (Genesis 41:12). I know a thing or two about being remembered late. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer before anybody came looking.

The answer is that he was restored to his position. The cupbearer says it himself: “I was restored to my position…” (Genesis 41:13). That's just what the young Hebrew had interpreted for him. He's back in his old position with Pharaoh, king of Egypt. That's a job comeback if I ever heard one.

The answer is True. Genesis 41:14 says “…Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon.” Joseph is the young Hebrew the cupbearer told him about. After two years in there, I think that was a very good morning.

The answer is that he says God will give the answer. Joseph says, “I myself cannot do it, but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer” (Genesis 41:16). Joseph, the young Hebrew, is standing in front of the king of Egypt. He points to God instead of himself. That's a humble answer in a big room.

The answer is False. Pharaoh says that after they devoured the well-fed cows, “…no one could tell that they had done so; their appearance was as ugly as it had been before.” (Genesis 41:21). It's one of the details he stresses to Joseph, the young Hebrew. Then he says he woke up.
The answer is False. Joseph says, “The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same.” (Genesis 41:25). He says it again in verse 26: “The dreams have the same meaning.” Two dreams, one message.

The answer is God. Joseph says, “God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do.” (Genesis 41:25). The dreams are about what God is about to do. Joseph, the young Hebrew, said earlier that God would give the answer (Genesis 41:16). He's staying consistent.

The answer is seven years of famine. That's what Joseph says. The seven thin cows and the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind “…are seven years of famine.” (Genesis 41:27). Seven good years, then seven hard ones. Joseph, the young Hebrew, makes the pattern clear.

The answer is False. Joseph says the abundance “…will be forgotten…” and “…will not be remembered…” once the famine arrives (Genesis 41:30-31). He says the famine will be that severe. I think this one is heavy, friends, so it's good that Joseph doesn't stop there. He goes on to say what Pharaoh can do to prepare.

The answer is that God decreed it and will do it shortly. Joseph says, “…because the dream was given to Pharaoh in two versions, the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly.” (Genesis 41:32). The two versions go with God having decreed it. Joseph, the young Hebrew, tells Pharaoh, king of Egypt, this directly.

The answer is a discerning and wise man. Joseph says, “…Pharaoh should look for a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt.” (Genesis 41:33). After laying out the dream, Joseph, the young Hebrew, moves on to what to do about it. This man is going to have a big job.

The answer is a fifth. Joseph says Pharaoh, king of Egypt, should “…appoint commissioners over the land to take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.” (Genesis 41:34). One out of every five. Joseph, the young Hebrew, is working out the numbers like he's done it before.

The answer is a reserve for the famine years. Joseph says, “This food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine to come upon the land of Egypt.” (Genesis 41:36). That's his plan: collect the excess food in the good years and lay up grain in the cities (Genesis 41:35). Save now, so the lean years don't catch the land empty-handed.

The answer is True. The stored food will be a reserve, “Then the country will not perish in the famine.” (Genesis 41:36). Joseph is the young Hebrew who stood in front of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and gave him both the warning and a plan. The grain is the difference.
